item.title: Adding a Child to Your Car Insurance? Here Are Ways to Hold Down the Costs.
item.description:
Car insurance is expensive, and insuring young adult drivers adds to the cost. But families do have options to manage the burden.

Unlike health insurance, a parent’s auto insurance policy has no required age cutoff for children. (The Affordable Care Act allows children to remain on a parent’s health plan until age 26. After that, they must have separate coverage.)

“It’s not an age question,” said Mark Friedlander, a spokesman for the Insurance Information Institute, an industry group. Rather, young drivers’ circumstances, such as where they live or whether they are students, come into play when considering separate coverage.

Douglas Heller, director of insurance at the Consumer Federation of America, an association of nonprofit consumer advocacy groups, agreed that there was no blanket answer. “It’s more situationally specific,” he said.

The question has been cropping up more often: A growing number of young adults live at home with their parents as they confront higher living costs and struggle to pay their student loans.

Here’s what to know, in general, about insurance for young adult drivers. Some details may vary by state and carrier, experts said, so it’s always best to confer with your insurance agent.

Drivers in their teens and early 20s have less experience behind the wheel and are at a higher risk for serious accidents.

That is why insurance premiums are highest for drivers in those age groups and generally become more affordable by age 25, said Julia Taliesin, an economic analyst with Insurify, a rate comparison and shopping site.

Inclusion on a family’s policy is often the most affordable option for young adult drivers, she said, because they can benefit from their parents’ lower risk rating and potentially from other factors, like their parents’ stronger credit history. (Most insurers consider credit-based scores when setting auto rates, arguing that they correlate with the likelihood of filing a claim. Seven states bar or restrict the practice.)

The average monthly premium for two parents with two cars that carry full coverage — liability, collision and comprehensive — is $243, according to Insurify data. Adding a 20-year-old who lives in the home to the policy increases the premium by an average of $210, to $453.

But if a 20-year-old had a separate policy, the average stand-alone premium would be $311.

Students living at home are generally eligible for coverage under their parents’ car insurance policy. Typically, all licensed drivers 16 or older living in a household are listed on the policy. It’s the policyholder’s responsibility to notify the insurer of eligible family members.

One possible exception: If the students are living at home and buy their own car and title it in their name, some insurers may require a separate policy unless a parent is added as a co-owner, Mr. Friedlander said.

If those students go away to college and take one of the parents’ cars with them, they are still considered a member of the household and can remain on their parents’ policy. That includes students attending graduate school — even extended programs, Mr. Friedlander said. “You could have a 40-year-old in the house” who is covered by the family policy, he said.

Students who don’t take a car with them to campus can also remain on the parents’ policy. “They come home for holidays and during the summer,” Mr. Friedlander said, and are covered during those periodic visits.

Yes. Families should ask their insurer if they are eligible for a so-called away at school discount if their child goes to college without a car, said Marguerita Cheng, a certified financial planner in Gaithersburg, Md., and a parent. Because those students won’t be driving the car much, their families qualify for a lower premium. Often, however, insurers offer the discount only if the student is attending a school at least 100 miles away from home, she said.

Another option, with potentially greater savings, is formally excluding the students from the family policy while they are away, Mr. Heller said. But the catch is that parents must remember to add the students back to the policy when they return home. Mr. Heller does this for a son who is in college and sets a reminder in his phone to add him when he returns home, he said.

Once children graduate, move out of the family home and take a car to a new, permanent address, “they should get their own policy,” said Robert Passmore, department vice president of personal lines at the American Property Casualty Insurance Association, an industry group.

That’s because the location where the car is kept is an important factor in setting insurance premiums, he said.

If the child moves to a more densely populated area where insurance costs are higher, it may be tempting to leave him or her on the family policy to avoid higher premiums at the new location. But there may be problems if a claim is filed and it becomes clear the car is housed elsewhere. “You can be canceled,” he said.

If the car is owned by a parent, it doesn’t necessarily have to be retitled in the adult child’s name, Mr. Passmore said. But doing so can help simplify things in the event of a claim. “If the car is totaled and in the parent’s name,” he said, “you have to sign all the paperwork.”

Families should speak with their children about auto insurance as soon as they get a license, said Christina Wing, a senior lecturer at Harvard Business School and author of “Unspeakable,” a guide to discussing sensitive subjects, including money. Parents, she said, can show their children the cost of adding them to their policy and explain that, while they are picking up the tab for now, eventually the child may be asked to contribute.

Parents can also set criteria for when their children go on their own insurance — ideally well in advance, so it doesn’t come as a surprise. “I never think you should just take it away,” she said. “It’s about readiness, not age.”

Scott Glasgow, executive director of FinMango, a nonprofit that promotes financial health among young adults and vulnerable communities, said parents might face their own financial pressures and need the child to help pay for coverage. “Parents can be squeezed as well,” he said.

Anthony Schilt, 24, a capital finance specialist in Columbus, Ohio, said his parents had him start paying his share of their car insurance policy — about $80 a month — when he was 18. He made the payments with income from various jobs, including one at a grocery store.

Mr. Schilt said he was thankful that his parents had given him the chance to start paying the premium to them first, rather than having to manage a separate policy on his own. “It helped me practice paying the bill,” he said.

After he was involved in an accident on an icy road when he was 19, he said, his parents’ policy premium jumped and they decided he should obtain his own coverage — a decision he said he had supported.

“I think the transition for young adults should be based on a trigger, not a birthday,” Mr. Schilt said. He gave examples like when children move into their own apartments or save enough money to cover the auto policy’s deductible and two months of premiums.

item.title: Networks to Resume White House Coverage After Standoff
item.description:
The major networks are set to resume their collective television coverage of President Trump on Friday, after a standoff that saw TV cameras go dark at the White House during the visit of China’s top leader.

CBS said it would serve as the television pool for Xi Jinping’s arrival at the White House at 10:30 a.m. Eastern, when Mr. Trump and the first lady will greet the Chinese leader and his wife.

And CNN said its cameras were set up at the National Archives, a museum that holds original copies of the Bill of Rights and the Constitution, where Mr. Trump will lead Mr. Xi for a visit around lunchtime.

The networks on Monday had suspended the TV pool, which provides video footage for daily presidential events, after Mr. Trump abruptly barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House. Those outlets regained access on Thursday after an order from a federal judge.

But the five networks that share pool duties — ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News and NBC — continued to stand down. They were seeking a written commitment from White House staff that CNN’s cameras would be allowed back into the pool rotation.

CNN received an email from the White House that included logistical instructions for Friday’s shoot at the National Archives, which the networks took as a de facto confirmation that the network would be allowed to proceed, according to three people briefed on internal discussions.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Without a TV pool in place, Mr. Xi’s pomp-filled visit to the White House has not been carried live on major American networks. Mr. Trump, in a social media post, described the visit as “Actually made for Television” and wrote that the networks had “refused” to cover it. The president did not mention that his administration had barred some outlets from the White House grounds.

A note to TV pool subscribers on Friday stressed that the networks could modify their plans depending on how the day played out.

“The plan is to return to covering the president in a normal capacity with a full crew,” the note said, according to a copy obtained by The New York Times. “This arrangement can be assessed throughout the day.”

Kristen Holmes, a White House correspondent for CNN, said on-the-air on Friday that pool coverage would restart. “We’ll actually see the president and President Xi on our TV screens,” she said.

item.title: Fed Confronts the Prospect of Another Rate Increase Ahead of Midterms
item.description:
When officials at the Federal Reserve raised interest rates last week in their first major step in years to turn the tide on inflation, many expected that it would buy the central bank time to see whether price pressures were easing before taking action again.

But over the course of the past week, a newfound urgency has been injected into the debate, raising the prospects that the central bank will be boxed into delivering another quarter-point increase at its next meeting in October.

That gathering is scheduled just days before midterm elections that will determine how much leeway President Trump will have to enact his agenda in the latter half of his term.

The Fed strives to be politically independent and asserts that it does not factor the electoral calendar into its policy debates. There are numerous instances in which the central bank either raised or lowered rates in the months leading up to or directly before an election because the economic conditions warranted it. But at a time when Mr. Trump has accused the Fed of being politically motivated and has taken direct aim at individual policymakers for not complying with his demands for substantially lower borrowing costs, the economic rationale needs to be ironclad.

Financial markets this week have boosted bets that the Fed will risk drawing Mr. Trump’s ire and proceed with another quarter-point increase that will lift rates to a new range of 4 percent to 4.25 percent at its meeting on Oct. 27-28. Traders in federal funds futures markets now ascribe roughly 70 percent odds on that outcome.

This belief stems from a string of data that has reinforced the view that the economy is gaining, not losing, momentum. The most recent evidence came from a closely- watched survey of the private sector by S&P Global, which on Wednesday showed that U.S. business activity surged to a five-year high in September. That followed in the wake of a robust retail sales report the week prior, and a stronger-than-expected jobs report earlier this month.

At the same time, the risks to inflation have shown few signs of subsiding. An impasse over ending the Iran war has kept the international price of oil stuck above $100 a barrel. The cost of a gallon of diesel has also shot higher, making it more expensive to manufacture and ship goods around the country. And the boom in spending on artificial intelligence shows little sign of abating.

Before its next gathering, the Fed will get another monthly jobs report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics and an update on the state of inflation as of September from the Consumer Price Index report, among other economic releases.

In the interim, Fed officials have come out in droves to convey that they are serious about quelling inflation, in keeping with a new set of projections released last week showing that they broadly supported at least one more quarter-point increase this year. After September’s rate decision, Kevin M. Warsh, the chairman, described the Fed’s action as removing a “dose of accommodation,” a framing that made clear the central bank would move again, but left open-ended just about everything else.

In the void, a range of views have emerged.

On Thursday, John C. Williams, who as president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York is vice-chair of the policy-setting committee, said it was “reasonable” to think that the central bank will have to raise rates again before year-end.

“But we have to see,” he said. ”We’re going to collect the data ​and do what we did between July and September.” That aligned with comments from the Philadelphia Fed’s Anna L. Paulson, another voting member this year, who said later on Thursday that “some modest further tightening may be warranted.”

Other officials conveyed much more certainty around the need to raise rates again to ensure that inflation retreats back to the Fed’s 2 percent target in a timely fashion. The Fed has overshot that target for more than five years.

Michael C. Barr, a Fed governor, said on Wednesday that further rate increases were necessary, having described the Fed’s previous policy settings as being “out of position.” That day, which also coincided with the release of the S&P Global report, the 10-year Treasury yield notched its biggest one-day jump since April 2025, when Mr. Trump announced sweeping global tariffs that he was later forced to unwind. It is now trading at its highest level in roughly 20 years, at nearly 5.2 percent.

Tom Barkin, president of the Richmond Fed, also this week leaned into the idea that the Fed would have to deliver more than one rate increase, citing the risk that “current elevated levels of inflation could affect future inflation.”

Perhaps the most sobering message came from Austan C. Goolsbee of the Chicago Fed, who warned that taming inflation could prove to be “painful.”

“Forcing inflation back to target in the short run means pushing employment below target,” said Mr. Goolsbee at an event in London on Monday. The unemployment rate stands at 4.1 percent.

After September’s rate decision, Jan Hatzius, chief U.S. economist at Goldman Sachs, changed his Fed forecast and added an October increase before an extended pause.

That reflected the strong signals being sent by officials that they wanted to soon get another increase “under their belt,” Mr. Hatzius said, rather than an acute economic need. “They’ve decided they want to deliver some firming, and that I think is most naturally delivered at consecutive meetings.”

By the Fed’s final meeting of the year in December, Mr. Hatzius expects inflation to have begun to ease in a much more meaningful way, so the rationale for skipping October only to raise rates in December “is going to be weaker from an economic perspective,” he said.

October’s decision is likely to come down to two factors, according to James Egelhof, chief U.S. economist at BNP Paribas. The first is whether incoming data ratifies the view that the economy is strong and inflation is not budging. The second revolves around the market’s perception of the Fed’s credibility and whether officials feel they can forgo a rate increase “without jeopardizing the confidence of investors and the public that they are committed to a return of inflation to 2 percent.”

Mr. Egelhof said the Fed “won the battle on credibility” when it raised rates in September, and reckons that the central bank will be “reluctant” to backslide by failing to follow through with an increase if markets are overwhelming expecting it in October.

This dynamic with markets has significant drawbacks for the Fed, especially if there starts to be a discrepancy between what is being priced in and what the central bank is prepared to do.

Part of the problem is that Mr. Warsh has decided to obscure his views on the trajectory for policy and what might cause it to shift. Without a clear framework for assessing the need for further increases, for example, the scope for markets to treat every month of solid data as justification for additional adjustments grows, said Marc Giannoni, chief U.S. economist for Barclays.

“If you don’t provide guidance to the market, the market can run away with it,” he said. “You need the Fed chair to anchor that one way or another.”
